title: Conditional syllogisms: the four forms and which are valid

blocks.text: A conditional syllogism starts with **If p, then q**, where p is the condition and q is what follows. The four forms differ only in the second premise. Using *If I study, I'll get a good grade*: **1** says I studied, so I'll get a good grade. **2** says I didn't get a good grade, so I didn't study. **3** says I got a good grade, so I studied. **4** says I didn't study, so I didn't get a good grade.

Form 1 is **modus ponens**: the condition is met, so what follows has to follow. Form 2 is **modus tollens**: if studying always leads to a good grade, then no good grade means no studying. Participants judged modus ponens correctly **97 percent** of the time but modus tollens only **60 percent**, even though both are valid.
children: Valid does not mean easy: modus tollens is much harder than modus ponens.

blocks.text: Form 3 is not valid because the first premise says what happens when someone studies, but not that studying is the only way to get a good grade. The same form with different content makes this clear: *If I live in Tucson then I live in Arizona; I live in Arizona; therefore I live in Tucson*. A person can live in Arizona without living in Tucson. Form 4 is not valid because the first premise says nothing about what happens when someone does not study, so a good grade could come another way. Only **40 percent** judged each of these correctly.
children: Both valid forms were judged correctly more often than both invalid forms.

title: Validity vs truth, belief bias and mental models

blocks.text: **Validity** is about form: a syllogism is valid if its conclusion follows logically from its premises. **Truth** is about whether the statements match the world. If a valid syllogism has true premises, its conclusion must be true. *All birds are animals; all animals have four legs; therefore all birds have four legs* is valid because it has the same form as the example with food, and its conclusion is false only because the second premise is false.
children: Valid does not guarantee a true conclusion.

blocks.text: Validity can fail even when everything sounds reasonable: *All of the students are tired; some tired people are irritable; therefore some of the students are irritable* is not valid. **Belief bias** is the tendency to think a syllogism is valid when its conclusion is believable, and **71 percent** of participants judged invalid syllogisms with believable conclusions as valid.
children: Judge whether the conclusion follows, not whether it sounds true.

blocks.text: How do you check validity? **Johnson-Laird (1999)** proposed **mental models**, specific situations represented in the mind. In the pool table problem, most people solve it by imagining how the balls are arranged. For syllogisms, you build a model of the premises, generate a tentative conclusion, then look for an exception where the premises are true but the conclusion is not. A conclusion is valid only if **no** model of the premises refutes it, so one exception is enough to reject it.
children: Do not stop at the first model that fits.

title: The Wason four-card problem: falsification and the permission schema

blocks.text: In the **Wason four-card problem**, the cards read E, K, 4 and 7, and the rule is *If there is a vowel on one side, then there is an even number on the other side*. The task is to turn over the minimum number of cards to test the rule. The correct answer is **E and 7**. Only **7 percent** chose the 7, while **46 percent** chose the 4, which is an error.
children: The 4 feels right, but it cannot break the rule whatever is on its back.

blocks.text: The **falsification principle** states that to test a rule you must look for situations that falsify it, meaning prove it false. A 7 with a vowel on its other side would break the rule, so turning it is a real test. Most participants fail to look for such cases.

The same logic is much easier with the rule *If drinking beer, then 21 years old* and cards reading Beer, Soda, 16 years old and 21 years old. **73 percent** answered correctly, because the only case that breaks the rule is someone drinking beer under 21, so the correct cards are **beer and 16 years old**. The explanation is the **permission schema**: if A is satisfied, B can be carried out, as with a drinking age. Context is important, but familiarity alone is not what helps.
children: The logic is identical; a familiar permission rule makes it easier to see what to check.

title: The framing effect and status quo bias (disease problem, opt-in and opt-out)

blocks.text: The **framing effect** is when decisions are influenced by how a decision is stated, even when the facts are the same. **Tversky and Kahneman (1981)** found that gain framing leads to **risk aversion** (the sure option) and loss framing leads to **risk taking** (the gamble).

In the disease problem, 600 people are expected to die. With the gain wording, **72 percent** chose Program A (200 saved for certain) over Program B (1/3 chance all saved, 2/3 chance none). With the loss wording, **78 percent** chose Program D (1/3 chance no one dies, 2/3 chance all die) over Program C (400 die for certain). But saving 200 of 600 means 400 die, so **A equals C and B equals D**.
children: Only the wording changed, and the majority switched from the sure option to the gamble.

blocks.text: The **status quo bias** is the tendency to do nothing when a decision is difficult. In opt-in countries a person must take a step to be an organ donor and consent is **under 28 percent**, while in opt-out countries a person is a donor unless they ask otherwise and consent is **over 99 percent**. Doing nothing makes you a non-donor under opt-in and a donor under opt-out.
children: In both cases the presentation, not the facts, drives the choice.

title: Emotions in decisions: expected and incidental emotions (Kermer, Lerner, Simonsohn, Sanfey)

blocks.text: Emotions take part in decision making and do not only get in its way. **Expected emotions** are the emotions people predict they will feel about an outcome, and they are one determinant of risk aversion. **Kermer and colleagues (2006)** showed that these predictions are inaccurate: people expected losing $3 to drop happiness about 4 points, but the real drop was about 1 point, because they ignore their coping mechanisms.
children: People overestimate how bad a loss will feel.

blocks.text: **Incidental emotions** are not specifically related to the decision, such as those from the surroundings or a recent experience. **Simonsohn (2007)** found applicants' academic attributes were weighted more heavily on cloudy days, and **Simonsohn (2009)** found visitors to a highly rated university were more likely to enroll if they visited on a cloudy day. **Lerner and colleagues (2004)** found that disgust lowered both selling and buying prices of highlighters, while sadness lowered the selling price but raised the buying price.
children: The mood or weather has nothing to do with the choice, yet it changes it.

blocks.text: **Sanfey and colleagues (2003)** used the ultimatum game. Utility theory says to accept any offer, but unfair offers like $8/$2 and $9/$1 were rejected more often from a human than from a computer, and more activation of the right anterior insula meant rejecting more offers, even though rejecting meant getting nothing.
children: Anger at unfairness can lead people to give up money.
